data.approach: Dynamic Programming with Least Significant Bit
data.key_insight: The number of set bits in a number i is equal to the number of set bits in i >> 1 plus the last bit (i & 1).

steps.title: Initialize DP table
steps.detail: Create an array ans of size n + 1 initialized to zeros, where ans[i] will store the number of 1-bits for integer i.

steps.title: Compute bit counts iteratively
steps.detail: Loop from 1 to n. For each i, use the relation ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1).

steps.title: Return the result
steps.detail: Return the fully populated ans list.

data.pattern_summary: Dynamic programming breaks a problem down into overlapping subproblems, storing the results of previous computations to build up solutions to larger ones.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: It fits because each number's bit count can be derived from a previously computed bit count using bit shifts.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: A hash map does not help here because we need sequential values from 0 to n rather than arbitrary key-value pairs.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers apply to sequences requiring inward traversal or sliding windows, which is not the case for counting bits.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Greedy makes locally optimal choices without looking back, whereas counting bits requires building on exact previous sub-results.

signals.phrase: each index i stores the number of set bits
signals.hint: Implies a sequential relationship where every index depends on a value computed earlier.
Limits us to visiting each number in a single pass without independent nested loops.

data.brute_force_idea: Loop from 0 to n, and for each number, repeatedly shift and count its bits from scratch.
data.brute_force_why: There are n numbers, and for each number, the while loop runs proportional to the number of bits, which is log(i).
data.bottleneck: The straightforward approach actually scales proportionally to n log n in the worst theoretical bit-length model, though for standard integers it runs efficiently.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how the bit count of a number relates to a smaller number you have already calculated.
Consider what happens when you shift a number to the right by one position.
Notice that i >> 1 gives a number whose bit count is already known.

data.overview: The algorithm computes the number of set bits for every number from 0 to n in O(n) time using dynamic programming. It builds the answer using the relation that any number i has the same bit count as i divided by 2, plus 1 if i is odd.
data.intuition: Think of finding the bit count of a number by looking at its shifted self. If you shift a number right by one, you drop its last bit; to find the current number's bit count, just take the shifted number's answer and add 1 if the dropped bit was a 1.

pitfalls: Forgetting that the array needs to be of size n + 1 to include n itself.
Off-by-one errors in the loop range, starting at 0 instead of 1.
Confusing operator precedence between bitwise shift and addition.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force solution repeatedly counts the bits of every number from scratch using division and modulo loops. The optimized solution removes this redundant work by reusing previously computed answers through bit shifting. Specifically, the number of set bits in any integer i is equal to the number of set bits in i >> 1 plus the least significant bit (i & 1).

derivation.note: Allocates the result array of size n + 1 once.
The loop runs n times to compute values from 1 to n.
Performs constant time O(1) bitwise operations and array lookups on each iteration.

data.time_summary: Line 3 takes O(n) space allocation time, line 4 runs a loop n times, and line 5 executes constant-time work inside that loop. Summing these up gives O(n) total time, which is confirmed by the step counts scaling linearly with n.
data.space_summary: The algorithm allocates a single list of size n + 1 to store the answer, resulting in O(n) extra space complexity.
data.takeaway: When computing properties for a sequence of numbers, check if the value for the current number can be derived in O(1) time from a previously computed smaller number using bit manipulation or arithmetic.
mistakes: Starting the loop at 0 instead of 1, which attempts an unnecessary bit shift on ans[0 >> 1].
Forgetting that integer division or bit shifting (i >> 1) cuts the number in half, making sub-problems directly available in the array.
Misinterpreting bitwise operators, such as confusing the right shift operator (>>) with the left shift operator (<<).
